question: Whether the existing positive-weight rule has a canonical all-zero limit

anchors.quote:
Allocate the remaining loss pro rata using pre-allocation carrying amounts.
If a proposed share exceeds an asset's reducible amount, assign only that
amount, remove that asset from the active set and redistribute the remainder
among the others. Repeat until the requested allocation is supplied or no
capacity remains. Each strict redistribution removes at least one asset, so
the finite procedure takes at most n saturation passes and one final split.
Use exact fractions in the teaching case; a future quantized profile needs
its own rounding/remainder rule and must not force a balancing plug.

On a qualified reversal, determine the new recoverable amount after a supported
change in estimates (114–116). Passage of time alone is insufficient. Exclude
goodwill (124). Each eligible asset's ceiling is the lower of its recoverable
amount if determinable and its carrying amount had no impairment occurred,
net of intervening depreciation (117/123). Missing assessment is unresolved;
an admitted inability to determine individual recoverable amount leaves the
no-impairment ceiling operative. Apply the same capped allocation to increases,
with positive current carrying amounts as weights (122).

A remaining reversal capacity shortfall is a recognition ceiling, not a liability
or authorization to restore goodwill. Preserve unit value and recognized
carrying amount separately. If an amount remains but every eligible asset has
zero carrying weight, this procedure returns `allocation_basis_unresolved`;
the standard's pro-rata instruction does not itself provide a unique positive
weight vector. Do not invent equal weights. That extension remains open.

122        A reversal of an impairment loss for a cash-generating unit shall be allocated to the assets of the unit,
           except for goodwill, pro rata with the carrying amounts of those assets. These increases in carrying
           amounts shall be treated as reversals of impairment losses for individual assets and recognised in
           accordance with paragraph 119.
123        In allocating a reversal of an impairment loss for a cash-generating unit in accordance with
           paragraph 122, the carrying amount of an asset shall not be increased above the lower of:
           (a)       its recoverable amount (if determinable); and
           (b)       the carrying amount that would have been determined (net of amortisation or depreciation)
                     had no impairment loss been recognised for the asset in prior periods.
           The amount of the reversal of the impairment loss that would otherwise have been allocated to the
           asset shall be allocated pro rata to the other assets of the unit, except for goodwill.

           Reversing an impairment loss for goodwill
124        An impairment loss recognised for goodwill shall not be reversed in a subsequent period.
125        AASB 138 Intangible Assets prohibits the recognition of internally generated goodwill. Any increase in the
           recoverable amount of goodwill in the periods following the recognition of an impairment loss for that
           goodwill is likely to be an increase in internally generated goodwill, rather than a reversal of the impairment
           loss recognised for the acquired goodwill.

## Local mathematical diagnosis

Let c_i be eligible non-goodwill carrying amounts before reversal, and R the
amount to allocate after the applicable unit-level findings. The ordinary
uncapped expression R c_i / sum_j c_j requires a positive denominator. If every
c_i is zero, the expression is undefined, rather than a prescribed zero
reversal or a direction to divide equally.

Caps do not generally repair this. With two assets, positive capacities m_1
and m_2 and 0 < R < m_1 + m_2, amounts satisfying the cap and total constraints
alone have x_1 in [max(0, R − m_2), min(m_1, R)] and x_2 = R − x_1. This
interval follows by substitution into 0 ≤ x_i ≤ m_i and has positive width
under those premises. At R = 0 or R = m_1 + m_2 it collapses; that mathematical
uniqueness still does not supply an authoritative allocation rule. These are
cap-compatible amounts, not a claim of IAS 36 admissibility. Choosing capacity
weights, pre-impairment weights or equal weights would add a policy not
established by the inspected passage.

The strongest tempting inference is to treat the all-zero case as a limiting
version of this ordinary allocation or to use restoration capacities as
weights. Neither inference is stated or derived in the inspected source.
Changing to a single-asset unit of account would also change the question.
